gloss: thousand; a clan (a tribe’s “thousand”); cattle; chief, close companion; learn, teach
summary: אֶלֶף is a thousand: a count of men, silver or cubits, and scripture’s round figure for a great many, as in mercy “to a thousand generations” and “a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday” (Deu 7:9; Psa 90:4). It is also a tribe’s “thousand”, a clan and the unit it musters under its head, so that “the heads of the thousands of Israel” answer the trumpet and Yahweh returns to “the myriads of the thousands of Israel” (Num 10:4, 36; Jdg 6:15; Mic 5:1). The same word in the plural is cattle (Deu 7:13; Psa 8:8), as Akkadian alpu and Ugaritic and Phoenician ʾlp are an ox. אַלּוּף is the chief of a clan (Gen 36) and a close companion (Pro 16:28; Psa 55:14), and the verb is to become used to, learn (Pro 22:25), and in the piel to teach (Job 33:33), as Arabic ʾalifa is to keep to and grow familiar with; how the thousand, the ox and the learning go back to one root the text does not show.

words.gloss: thousand; a tribe’s “thousand”, a clan or its muster
words.summary: The numeral a thousand, with the dual אַלְפַּיִם two thousand and the plural for thousands; and by a use the Pentateuch, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Micah share, a “thousand” of a tribe: a clan, the division a tribe is mustered by, under its own head.

senses.definition: The number a thousand, counting people, animals, weights and measures; with other numerals for the great totals of the musters and spoils, dual אַלְפַּיִם two thousand.

evidence.note: “A thousand of a tribe, a thousand of a tribe, of all the tribes of Israel you shall send to the war.”
“A thousand of a tribe, twelve thousand armed for war”: twelve tribes, twelve thousand.

The sea held אַלְפַּיִם, two thousand, baths.

senses.gloss: a thousand: a unit of the muster under its captain

doctrine.statement: Yahweh describes himself as “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exo 20:5–6; Deu 5:9–10). Moses explains the thousands as generations: “the faithful God, who keeps covenant and kindness with those who love him … to a thousand generations” (Deu 7:9), and the psalm says the covenant with Abraham is “the word he commanded to a thousand generations” (Psa 105:8–10; 1Ch 16:15–17). Three or four set against a thousand: his kindness to those who love him outlasts his judgment of those who hate him beyond all comparison, and the promise to Abraham stands for as long as there are generations to receive it.

Moses prays, “a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday when it is past, and a watch in the night” (Psa 90:4), set against man’s seventy or eighty years (90:10). Peter takes it up against those who scoff that the promise of Christ’s coming has failed: “one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day; the Lord is not slow concerning his promise … but is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish” (2Pe 3:3–9). The verses say that the length of the wait is no measure of the promise’s certainty, and that the delay is God’s patience. They are not a rule for turning days into thousands of years: the same Moses wrote the six days of creation as days, each with its evening and morning, and the sabbath law rests on them as days (Gen 1:5, 31; Exo 20:11).

When Elijah thought he alone was left, Yahweh answered, “I have left seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal” (1Ki 19:14, 18). Paul quotes it, “I have kept for myself seven thousand men”, and applies it: “so too at the present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:2–5). A thousand here is the count of the faithful God keeps when they seem to be none: the remnant is his doing, kept by him, and larger than the one who mourns can see.

Micah says of Bethlehem Ephrathah that it is “little to be among the thousands of Judah”, the clans by which the tribe was numbered, yet “from you shall come out to me one to be ruler in Israel” (Mic 5:1). When Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests and scribes answered from this verse, “in Bethlehem of Judea”, and Matthew renders the thousands by their chiefs, “by no means least among the princes of Judah” (Mat 2:4–6). Jesus was born there because Joseph “was of the house and lineage of David” (Luk 2:4–7). The smallness of Bethlehem’s clan is the point of the prophecy: the ruler comes from the least of Judah’s thousands, as David, the youngest of his father’s house, had come from it before him (1Sa 16:11–13; 17:12).
